summary: In a vision Abram raises his lack of a child, and Yahweh promises an heir from Abram’s own body and descendants as countless as the stars. A ritual with divided animals accompanies a troubling forecast of foreign servitude and return, and Yahweh makes a covenant promising a named territory to Abram’s descendants.
whyItMatters: The chapter joins faith and promise to delay, affliction, and the presence of other peoples in the promised land. It anticipates the family’s future in Egypt while keeping Abram’s own unanswered question about land visible.

context.author: Genesis names no historical writer. Jewish and Christian tradition associates the Torah with Moses; the book briefing describes older traditions shaped into a final literary form, without a settled account of every stage.
context.audience: The book addresses Israel through a story of shared human origins and the family from whom Israel traces its ancestry; no single first audience is named in this chapter.
context.date: The narrated events belong to primeval or ancestral time, not to a securely dated writing event. Major stages of Genesis are often placed across the monarchic to Persian periods, with exact models and dates debated.
context.setting: Abram’s visionary encounter, an outdoor view of stars, and the arranged animal pieces at sunset.
context.literaryForm: Vision dialogue about heir and land, ritual scene, future oracle, and covenant land list.

before.text: Abram has returned from rescuing Lot, accepted Melchizedek’s blessing, and refused Sodom’s goods. A new vision addresses fear and reward.

here.text: Abram asks about both child and land; the answers promise descendants but also forecast generations of foreignness and affliction.

after.text: Sarai and Abram seek a child through Hagar, Sarai’s Egyptian servant, leading to conflict and Hagar’s flight.

outline.heading: Fear, childlessness, and promised heir
outline.note: Abram asks who will inherit; Yahweh promises a bodily descendant and many offspring.

outline.heading: Land question and animal preparation
outline.note: Abram asks how he will know the land is his; he arranges divided animals.

outline.heading: Darkness and forecast of foreign service
outline.note: The descendants’ future affliction and return are disclosed, along with Abram’s death notice.

outline.heading: Passing fire and territorial covenant
outline.note: A fiery presence passes between pieces as Yahweh names land and peoples.

keyVerses.text: He believed in Yahweh, who credited it to him for righteousness.
keyVerses.why: Abram’s trust is credited as righteousness within the heir dialogue.

keyVerses.text: He said to Abram, “Know for sure that your offspring will live as foreigners in a land that is not theirs, and will serve them. They will afflict them four hundred years.
keyVerses.why: The promise includes a difficult future of foreign residence and affliction.

keyVerses.text: In that day Yahweh made a covenant with Abram, saying, “I have given this land to your offspring, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates:
keyVerses.why: The covenant statement names the land promise and broad boundaries.

questions.question: What problem does Abram bring into the vision?
questions.answer: He says he remains childless and expects someone from his household, Eliezer, to inherit. Yahweh answers that an heir from Abram’s own body will come, then points to the stars as an image for offspring.

questions.question: What does “credited it to him for righteousness” say here?
questions.answer: The verse reports that Abram believes Yahweh’s promise and Yahweh counts that trust as righteousness. It does not give a full later doctrine of righteousness or list a series of works that earned the promise.

questions.question: Why does Abram ask “How will I know?” after believing?
questions.answer: His belief follows the offspring promise, while his next question concerns inheriting the land. The chapter places trust and an unresolved land question in the same encounter rather than treating every question as unbelief.

questions.question: What is a “heifer” in the ritual instructions?
questions.answer: It is one of the animals Yahweh tells Abram to bring, alongside a goat, ram, turtledove, and pigeon. Abram divides the larger animals and lays the pieces opposite each other, while leaving the birds whole.

questions.question: Why does a promise to Abram include the affliction of his descendants?
questions.answer: Yahweh says they will be foreigners and servants in another land for four hundred years before that nation is judged and they leave. The passage predicts suffering within the promise but does not say that enslaving them is morally acceptable.

questions.question: What does “the iniquity of the Amorite is not yet full” explain?
questions.answer: It is given as a reason the descendants’ return to the land lies later rather than immediately. The line names a moral judgment but gives no detailed account of every Amorite person or permission for readers to condemn present peoples.

questions.question: Who passes between the divided pieces?
questions.answer: After darkness falls, the narrative describes a smoking furnace and flaming torch passing between them, and then says Yahweh makes a covenant. It does not say Abram himself walks that path in the scene.

questions.question: Does the land list erase the peoples already named there?
questions.answer: No. The covenant names a wide territory and then lists existing peoples associated with it. The chapter does not narrate their removal or supply a modern territorial claim; the tension is part of this ancestral promise.

glossary.def: The person who would inherit Abram’s estate, central because Abram has no child.
A female cow among the animals prepared for the covenant scene.
The people named in the delayed-return explanation and again in the land list.
